text: Real Bitcask writes a 'hint' file next to each data file holding just the keys and their positions. On startup it rebuilds the in-memory keydir from these small hint files instead of scanning the full data files, which shortens recovery a lot.
why: Shows how the slow index rebuild the class accepted is fixed in practice.

text: Riak's Bitcask defaults to sync_strategy = none, which leaves flushing to the operating system. A process crash loses nothing, but a power or OS failure before the flush can lose recent writes; o_sync forces a flush on every write at a throughput cost.
why: Per-write durability is a setting, not automatic, even in Bitcask.

text: Riak's Bitcask rotates data files at max_file_size, 2 GB by default: when a write would push the active file past the limit, the file is closed and a new one opened.
why: Gives a real-world value for the rotation threshold.

text: Riak's Bitcask triggers merges by how much garbage exists rather than on a fixed clock: by default a merge starts when a file has 60% dead keys or 512 MB of dead bytes, and files join a merge at 40% dead keys or 128 MB of dead bytes. A merge window can restrict merges to off-peak hours.
why: Shows how the 'merge frequency' knob is actually expressed.

text: In Bitcask's source each entry is written as CRC32, timestamp, key size, value size, key, value, and the CRC32 is computed over everything after it. The reader decodes the same order and re-checks the CRC.
why: Confirms the taught record format against the real implementation.

text: LevelDB's log format also starts each record with a CRC32C. When the reader finds corrupted data it skips it and resynchronises at the next block boundary rather than trying to repair it.
why: A second production engine that uses the 'skip corrupt entries' heuristic.

text: PostgreSQL protects each WAL record with a CRC-32C. The CRC is set when the record is written and checked during crash recovery, archive recovery and replication.
why: Gives the correct Postgres example of record-level integrity checks.

text: MySQL's binlog_checksum defaults to CRC32, so the server writes a checksum for each binary log event. The checksum is the last 4 bytes of the serialized event.
why: Correct MySQL example; the checksum is at the end, not the start.

text: PostgreSQL writes 8 KB pages, i.e. 16 sectors of 512 bytes, and a power loss can leave some sectors written and others not. To survive this it logs full page images to the WAL (full_page_writes), which can be turned off on file systems such as ZFS that prevent partial page writes.
why: Concrete example of how a real database handles non-atomic writes.

text: S3 serves one byte range per GET (Range: bytes=start-end); it does not return multiple ranges in a single request. Concurrent ranged GETs are AWS's recommended way to download large objects quickly.
why: Exact capability the pointed-read design relies on, plus its limit.

text: AWS says small S3 requests usually see median latencies in the tens of milliseconds, and recommends a cache (ElastiCache, CloudFront) in front of S3 for frequently read data.
why: Quantifies 'S3 is slow' for the hot/cold tier decision.

text: An Apache Hudi index maps each record key (optionally with partition path) to the file id holding it. Bloom-filter and record-level indexes in the metadata table let upserts and point lookups avoid scanning every data file.
why: Clarifies what the Hudi index actually stores.

text: In Cassandra's write path every write goes first to the on-disk commit log, then to the in-memory memtable. Memtables are flushed to SSTables, which are immutable and never written again; with the default periodic commit-log sync (10 s) a crash can lose up to that window.
why: Correct picture of what an LSM keeps in memory versus on disk.

text: In Riak each key is hashed onto a ring split into partitions owned by vnodes, and a write goes to the owning vnode and the vnodes for the next N-1 partitions. Any node can coordinate a request: there is no master node.
why: Corrects the master-slave picture of Riak.

text: Linux keeps file data that has been read in the page cache, so later reads of nearby bytes are served from memory without another disk access.
why: Explains why byte-at-a-time reads cost calls, not disk I/Os.

text: SQLite is the classic serverless engine: the application process reads and writes the database file directly, with no separate server process.
why: Makes 'embedded database' concrete with an official definition.

text: Zoned storage exposes a flash property directly: a zone must be written sequentially and erased (reset) before it can be overwritten. SSDs adopt this interface to reduce write amplification, which is why append-only layouts still help on flash.
why: Shows why append-only still helps on SSDs.
